title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
summary: You get a list `heights` that describes a bar chart: bar i has height `heights[i]` and width 1, and the bars stand side by side with no gaps. A rectangle drawn inside the chart covers a run of adjacent bars and can be no taller than the shortest bar in that run. Return the largest area such a rectangle can have.

examples.explanation: The bars at indexes 1 to 3 (heights 4, 5 and 3) hold a rectangle of height 3 and width 3.
The tall bar alone wins: any wider rectangle has to drop to height 2 or 1.

approaches.twist: Keep indexes of rising heights on a stack; when a shorter bar pops one, that bar's rectangle fills the gap between the new top and the shorter bar.
Try every run of bars: fix a start, move the end right while tracking the shortest height, and keep the best area.
approaches.note: Works, but trying every run of bars takes O(n²) time, far too slow for 10⁵ bars. The target is O(n).

signals.meaning: Try each bar as the shortest one: its rectangle stretches left and right until a shorter bar stops it. A stack of rising heights finds both stopping bars in one pass.
A run's width is a difference of positions, so keep indexes on the stack, not heights; enumerate() gives each bar's index and height together.

constraintReading: Up to 10⁵ bars: trying every run is O(n²), about 5·10⁹ runs, far too slow. O(n) means each bar is pushed once and popped once, and the pop finds its shorter neighbor on each side; the stack can hold every index, so the space is O(n).

related.relation: Also keeps indexes on a stack, but in rising order: a shorter bar pops taller ones and measures their rectangles, where a warmer day pops colder ones.
